## 1. Introduction  

<|ref|>text<|/ref|><|det|>[[114, 108, 883, 230]]<|/det|>
The ubiquitous photodetector plays a critical role in nearly all areas of science and technology. They are central to a wide range of optoelectronic technologies, including optical communication, imaging, biosensing, and wearable devices. [1] As applications increasingly demand devices that are energy- efficient, low- cost, and capable of detecting across a wide spectral range, the development of photodetectors with broadband responses and high sensitivity has become an important research priority.  

<|ref|>text<|/ref|><|det|>[[113, 228, 883, 530]]<|/det|>
In addition to basic photoelectric conversion, photodetectors exhibit wavelength- dependent carrier transport. This phenomenon arises from the spectral dependence of the semiconductor absorption coefficient \(\alpha (\lambda)\) , which governs the depth of photon penetration into the device. Because the carrier transit time is directly linked to the absorption depth, incremental changes in the wavelength can produce measurable variations in carrier transport. As illustrated in Fig. 1, a slight increase in the wavelength of illumination causes its penetration depth to either approach the junction (for sufficiently short wavelengths, \(\lambda_{l}\) ) or recede from the junction (for longer wavelengths, \(\lambda_{2}\) ). This results in either a reduction or an increase in the average charge carrier transit time and phase delay of the modulated photocurrent. In this manner, each wavelength component of the illumination generates electron- hole pairs at different depths, and their subsequent drift and diffusion contribute to the RF amplitude and phase \(\Omega \tau\) of the photocurrent, where \(\Omega = 2\pi f\) is the angular frequency, and \(\tau\) is the effective carrier transit time. This effect, known as Optoelectronic Chromatic Dispersion (OED). [2,3] is the basis for photodiode- only, compact, high- resolution wavelength sensors and spectroscopic tools. By sweeping across the RF frequency range, the complete optical spectrum can be reconstructed. [4- 8]  

<|ref|>text<|/ref|><|det|>[[113, 529, 884, 799]]<|/det|>
A change in optical wavelength \(\Delta \lambda\) , changes the effective carrier transit time, \(\Delta \tau\) . This wavelength dependance is characterized by the OED dispersion coefficient, \(\widehat{D}_{OED} = \frac{\Delta\tau}{\Delta\lambda}\) so a change in optical wavelength produces a modulation phase delay \(\Delta \theta = \Omega \widehat{D}_{OED}\Delta \lambda\) . The OED sensitivity, defined as the phase change per unit wavelength change, is therefore \(S_{OED} = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta\lambda} = \Omega \widehat{D}_{OED}\) . [2,3] As explained above, and with reference to Fig. 1, the sign and magnitude of the OED sensitivity depend on the location of carrier generation relative to the junction. The magnitude of OED sensitivity is proportional to \(\alpha^{- 1}\frac{d\alpha}{d\lambda}\) , i.e., penetration depth and the slope of the absorption dispersion. [3] The magnitude of the OED dispersion coefficient is enormous over wide spectral regions, comparable to the dispersion exhibited by hundreds of kilometers of optical fibers under the same modulation frequencies. [9] The OED response can be enhanced, suppressed, or tuned for specific applications through appropriate choices of materials, intrinsic layer thickness, doping [10], and photodiode working point [11].  

<|ref|>text<|/ref|><|det|>[[114, 798, 883, 899]]<|/det|>
Based on this physical picture, prior research has shown that OED enables highly sensitive wavelength detection. Ge PN devices exhibit a large dispersion in the C- and L- bands, enabling precise wavelength monitoring and FBG interrogation using a single detector. [12] Electronic enhancement techniques later increased the sensitivity to the femtometer scale, and additional studies utilized OED for material sensing.
